slides.headline: The world's largest lizard has a venomous bite.
slides.sub: It is not just bacteria. Researchers found venom glands in the Komodo dragon's lower jaw

slides.label: long: the largest living lizard species
slides.body: A Komodo dragon weighs about 135 kg. The largest individuals, often males, can weigh as much as 165 kg.

slides.headline: Venom glands in the lower jaw
slides.body: Researchers found a venom gland with six compartments in the lower jaw. Separate ducts open between the serrated teeth.

slides.headline: What the venom does
slides.body: It stops blood from clotting and lowers blood pressure. Bitten prey bleeds heavily and goes into shock.

slides.headline: Wounds and bacteria count too
slides.body: Herpetologists note that the physical trauma of the bite and bacteria from the mouth also play large roles in slowing and killing prey.

slides.label: mature individuals recorded on the IUCN Red List
slides.body: Status: Endangered. Assessed in 2019 and published in 2021. The population trend is listed as stable.

caption:
The Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis) is the largest living lizard, and its bite delivers venom.

It lives on Komodo and a few neighbouring islands in Indonesia. The 2009 study found a relatively weak skull and a low bite force, and pointed to its serrated teeth and its venom instead. At times it can smell carrion up to 4 km away, and an adult can eat up to 80 percent of its own body weight in one meal.

Swipe for how the bite works. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Fry et al. (2009), PNAS 106:8969–8974; Britannica; Smithsonian's National Zoo; IUCN Red List (assessed 2019, published 2021).
